talks.title: On the Coalgebraic Linear-Time Semantics of Two-Player Games
talks.speaker: Ben Plummer
talks.description: Linear-time semantics play an important role in program semantics and verification, in settings where branching-time equivalence is too fine. Set-based coalgebra provides an account of branching-time behaviour, while finite linear-time semantics can be treated coalgebraically by moving to the Kleisli category of a monad modelling the system’s branching. In this talk, I will discuss how these ideas extend to the linear-time semantics of two-player games. For finite behaviour, the coalgebraic approach applies smoothly to games in which the opponent’s choices are nondeterministic, probabilistic, or weighted. We characterise the resulting semantics in terms of strategies that enforce…

talks.title: Mysteries of matter: new experiments to unpick the nature of dark matter
talks.speaker: Dr Daniel Johnson
talks.location: Poynting Large Lecture Theatre, Physics Building (R13)
talks.description: Contrary to its name, there is nothing hidden about dark matter. It's there in plain sight, dramatically changing the way galaxies move and imprinted all over the incredible pictures astronomers take of the cosmos. But, whilst we know for sure that it is there, we have no idea what it's made of and that makes particle physicists deeply uncomfortable. This evening we will explore new methods to tease out truths about the particle identity of dark matter, and how new experiments might soon shed light on this mysterious matter that, overwhelmingly, dominates the 'stuff' in the Universe.

talks.title: Semantics and intermediate representations of probabilistic programs
talks.speaker: Hugo Paquet
talks.description: In a probabilistic programming language (with only finite types and without recursion or loops) every program determines a probability distribution over a set of outputs. Computing this distribution can be expensive: the naive approach is to enumerate all possible executions. So practical interpreters rely on more efficient representations of probability distributions, typically inspired by symbolic execution. In this talk I will give a semantic perspective on these intermediate representations, to explain why they are correct. talks.description: The algebraic effects and handlers paradigm separates the concerns of the interface and implementation of computational effects in programming languages. talks.description: At the High-Luminosity LHC, LHCb Upgrade II will record about 25 proton–proton collisions per bunch crossing. talks.description: Here is a popular challenge: Can you copy a given drawing without lifting your pen or tracing any line more than once? (In this talk, we focus on Eulerian cycles, where the endpoints of the trail are equal.) talks.title: The finitary aspects of Full Ground Local State
talks.speaker: Orpheas van Rooij
talks.description: Full ground local state (FGLS) refers to dynamically allocated mutable state that allows storing ground values and references. It is a key ingredient in many imperative algorithms as it enables cyclic data structures. In this work, we focus on one particular denotational model for FGLS: Kammar et al.'s possible worlds monad on sets indexed over sets of locations. We resolve an outstanding question about this FGLS monad: is it finitary? We show that it is not, by showing the existence of non-finitary computations in this monad that are challenging to define in a terminating language with full ground references. talks.speaker: Dr Jenni French
talks.location: Poynting Large Lecture Theatre, Physics Building (R13)
talks.description: Brown dwarfs are the Universe’s awkward middle child, not quite a star, not quite a planet, but they are fascinating in their own right. Acting as the intermediary objects between planets and stars, brown dwarfs have complex atmospheres and act as natural laboratories for a plethora of exoplanet science. This talk explores brown dwarfs, what they are, how we find them, and why they’re so interesting, as well as how you can get involved in their discovery.

talks.title: Weak Boson Scattering at the Large Hadron Collider, Circa 2030 and Beyond.
talks.description: The Large Hadron Collider (LHC) is a remarkable multipurpose accelerator complex. With a proton-proton center-of-mass energy of 14 TeV, it allows one to study directly, in a laboratory setting, the scattering of elementary particles at energies well beyond the electroweak scale. This include the scattering of two incoming W or Z bosons, a process known as "weak boson scattering" or more broadly as "vector boson scattering" (VBS). While long predicted, these ultra rare processes were observed for the first time only during Run II and III of the LHC's operation, and will be a physics driver of the high-luminosity (HL-LHC) program.In this talk, I will give a broad overview of the status and…

talks.title: Algebraically free Markov chains
talks.speaker: Paolo Perrone
talks.description: Algebraically free monoids, and more generally monads, are commonly used to model operations that can be 'folded', such as repeated actions of a set of 'elementary moves'. Notable examples are the writer monad (free over the alphabet set), and the free monad over a graph. talks.title: Seeing the invisible: Using light as a tool of discovery
talks.speaker: Dr George Smetana
talks.location: Poynting Large Lecture Theatre, Physics Building (R13)
talks.description: The human body is a surprisingly good instrument for scientific discovery, with our senses able to act as probes of the physics going on all around us. However, over time we've reached the limit of our experience living at an 'average' scale - too big to easily experience quantum phenomena and too small to comprehend the workings of the universe on cosmic scales. We've developed tools to help us, and the detection and manipulation of light has become one of the most important ones. I will share with you some of the surprising ways that we can use light in modern physics, even to detect the invisible.

talks.title: How to Film the Life of an Electron
talks.speaker: Dr Tom Siday
talks.location: Poynting Large Lecture Theatre, Physics Building (R13)
talks.description: Everything around you — your phone, solar panels, computers, the screen you're reading this on — works because of electrons zipping around inside materials. But catching them in the act is absurdly hard: they move in millionths of a billionth of a second, across distances smaller than a single atom. No ordinary camera comes close.In this talk, I'll show how we are building what amounts to the world's fastest and best-resolved camera, using some of the shortest possible flashes of light to photograph matter atom by atom at their native timescales. We're getting close to a long-standing dream: recording real-time movies of the fastest processes in nature.
